blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Look up at night. There is the moon. The moon is round and bright. But the moon does not make its own light. The sun shines on it. That is why it glows. The moon goes around and around the Earth. It turns slowly as it goes. So we always see the same side. The moon has a back we never see. No one standing on Earth has ever seen it. Spaceships have. They flew all the way around and took pictures of it.

blocks.prompt: The Moon Only Shows Us One Face
blocks.text: The moon is our neighbor in space. It is a big ball of rock. It goes around the Earth once a month. The moon looks bright, but it does not glow on its own. It is really gray, like an old road. The sun lights it up, the way a lamp lights up your face in a dark room. Here is the strange part. The moon spins slowly as it circles us. It spins just fast enough that the same side always points at Earth. The other side stays hidden. People on Earth watched the moon for thousands of years and never once saw its back.

blocks.prompt: The Side Nobody Had Seen
blocks.text: For as long as people have looked up, the Moon has shown us the same face. The dark patches make the same shapes every night. Your great-great-grandparents saw the exact same Moon face that you see. Nobody planned this. It happens because the Moon spins. It turns around once every time it circles the Earth, and those two motions match perfectly. Imagine walking a full circle around a chair while always keeping your eyes on it. You turn all the way around, but the chair only ever sees your front. The Moon does that to us. In 1959, a small Soviet spacecraft called Luna 3 flew behind the Moon and took the first photographs of the hidden side. The pictures were blurry. They were also a shock. The near side is covered in wide dark plains of old hardened lava. The far side has almost none. It is crowded with craters instead, rough and pale and beaten up. The two halves of the Moon do not match, and scientists are still working out why.

4.title: The Moon Only Shows Us One Face
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10

meta.templateLabel: The Moon Only Shows Us One Face

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Tidal locking: it spins once per orbit
Gravity stretches the Moon into an egg shape
The Moon drifts 3.8 cm farther away each year
Apollo crews left mirrors for measuring with lasers
Its gravity is about one sixth of Earth's
Ocean tides are the same force working in reverse

blocks.prompt: Locked in Step
blocks.text: The Moon has not always shown us one face. Billions of years ago it spun much faster, turning several times during each trip around the Earth. Anyone standing on the early Earth would have watched the whole Moon rotate past, front and back. Then gravity went to work. Earth pulls on the Moon, and it does not pull evenly. The near side of the Moon feels a slightly stronger tug than the far side, so the whole body of the Moon stretches a little into an egg shape. When the Moon spun, that bulge had to keep shifting through the rock to stay pointed at Earth, and shifting rock creates friction. Friction bleeds away energy. Over millions of years the spin slowed, and slowed, until the Moon turned exactly once per orbit. Then the bulge no longer had to move, the friction stopped, and the Moon settled there. Scientists call this tidal locking, and it is common. Almost every large moon in the solar system is locked to its planet. The same force works on us in reverse. The Moon tugs Earth's oceans into bulges, which we call tides, and the friction of those tides is slowly slowing Earth's spin. That energy has to go somewhere, and it goes into the Moon's orbit, pushing the Moon steadily outward. Astronauts left mirrors on the surface, and lasers fired at them from Earth measure the distance exactly. The answer: the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away every year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow.

answers: (spinning once per orbit, so the same face always points at the planet)
the bulge had to keep shifting through the rock, and that friction bled away energy

(inference: the distance is huge and the change is tiny, so they needed an exact way to measure it)

blocks.prompt: Why the Two Halves Do Not Match
blocks.text: Ask someone to draw the Moon and they will draw the face we know: bright highlands broken by wide dark patches. Those patches are called maria, from the Latin word for seas, because the first astronomers with telescopes assumed they were oceans. They are not water. They are basalt, hardened floods of lava that welled up through the crust billions of years ago and pooled in enormous impact basins. Maria cover roughly a third of the near side. On the far side they cover about one percent. That difference is one of the strangest facts in the solar system, and it needs explaining. The leading answer starts with the Moon's birth. About 4.5 billion years ago, when the solar system was still a shooting gallery, a body roughly the size of Mars struck the young Earth. The collision threw a vast plume of vaporized rock into orbit, and out of that glowing ring the Moon assembled itself. The evidence is chemical. Moon rock and Earth rock share nearly identical oxygen isotopes, as if they were cut from the same cloth, and the Moon carries only a small iron core because most of the iron stayed behind inside Earth. Then the Moon locked into step with us, and the locking may explain the lopsidedness. Because the near side has always faced an Earth that was, at the beginning, still glowing with the heat of the impact, that hemisphere stayed warmer for longer. The far side radiated its heat into empty space, cooled faster, and built a thicker crust, in places more than twice the depth. Later, when magma tried to rise, it broke through the thin near-side crust easily and flooded the basins there. On the far side it mostly could not get out. The result is a Moon with two personalities: one smooth and dark and turned toward us, one pale and battered and permanently turned away. Nobody knew this until 1959, when Luna 3 sent back its grainy photographs, and half the Moon stopped being a mystery and started being a puzzle.

6.title: The Moon Only Shows Us One Face
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Moon Only Shows Us One Face

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Diameter 3,475 km, about a quarter of Earth's
Libration lets us see about 59% of the surface
There is no permanently dark side
Retreating 3.8 cm per year, measured by laser
The Sun is about 400x wider and about 400x farther away
Luna 3 saw the far side first, in 1959

blocks.prompt: The Face We Were Given
blocks.text: There is no dark side of the Moon. The phrase is one of the most successful errors in the English language. Every part of the Moon's surface receives sunlight, and the far side gets exactly as much as the side you can see, just on a different schedule. What the far side lacks is not light. It is us. It has never had a view of Earth, and until 1959 Earth had never had a view of it. The reason is a slow, patient piece of physics called tidal locking. Earth's gravity does not pull on the Moon evenly. The near side is closer, so it feels a stronger tug, and the Moon's whole body is stretched slightly along the line between us. Early in its history the Moon spun quickly, which meant that stretched bulge had to travel continuously through the rock to stay aimed at Earth. Flexing rock generates friction, friction drains rotational energy, and after some millions of years the spin had bled down to a single turn per orbit. At that point the bulge no longer had to move. The system reached its lowest-energy arrangement and stopped there. This is not a coincidence and it is not rare. Nearly every large moon in the solar system is locked to its planet, for exactly the same reason. The lock is not perfect. The Moon's orbit is slightly elliptical, so it speeds up and slows down as it travels, while its rotation stays steady. The two fall in and out of step, and the Moon appears to rock gently back and forth, a motion called libration. Over the course of a month that rocking lets us peek a little way around each edge. Add up the peeking and we can see about 59 percent of the surface from Earth. The remaining 41 percent stayed genuinely unseen until Luna 3 flew behind it, and what came back was not the Moon anyone expected. The near side is dominated by maria, dark basalt plains that flooded ancient impact basins and cover roughly a third of the hemisphere. The far side has barely one percent. It is instead a crowded field of craters, pale and unrelieved. The best explanation ties back to the locking. Because the Moon has always faced an Earth that was, at the beginning, still glowing from the impact that created the Moon in the first place, the near side stayed hot for longer. The far side radiated its heat into empty space and built a thicker crust, in places double the depth. When magma later rose, it broke through the thin side easily and never made it through the thick one. The Moon we look at and the Moon we do not are two different worlds, and the difference exists because of which way it happened to be pointed. None of this is decoration. The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's diameter, which is absurd for a planet our size, and that mass acts as a gyroscopic anchor. Many scientists argue that without it, Earth's tilt would wander far more than the couple of degrees it currently wobbles, and our seasons would wander with it. The same tides that locked the Moon are also, in reverse, slowing us down. Earth's day is lengthening by a fraction of a second per century, and the rotation we lose is handed to the Moon's orbit. Mirrors left on the surface by Apollo crews let us measure the result with lasers. The Moon is retreating from us at 3.8 centimeters a year. Which means the sky you were born under is temporary. Right now the Moon and the Sun happen to appear almost exactly the same size from Earth, because the Sun is about four hundred times wider and about four hundred times farther away. That coincidence is the only reason a total solar eclipse is possible. It is also expiring. Given enough time the Moon will be too far away to cover the Sun completely, and the last total eclipse on Earth will happen without an audience that knows it is the last. We arrived in the narrow window when the arithmetic works.
